title: Stroke
summary: Possible stroke: check FAST, write down when the signs started, get help and start evacuating now, no aspirin, sugar only for possible low blood sugar in someone fully awake who swallows safely, side position if drowsy or drooling.

steps.text: Check: do they respond? Are they breathing normally?
steps.detail: Gasping or occasional breaths are not normal breathing. If you are not sure, treat it as not breathing normally.

ask.q: Are they unresponsive and not breathing normally?

steps.text: Check FAST. Face: ask them to smile; does one side droop? Arms: ask them to raise both; does one drift down? Speech: ask them to repeat a simple sentence; is it slurred or wrong?
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (Class 1) recommends a stroke recognition scale such as FAST (Face, Arms, Speech, Time). The Red Cross lay page and MedlinePlus also use FAST; none of the sources opened uses BE-FAST. How to check each part is from MedlinePlus.

Time: any one of these signs, appearing suddenly, means act now.

Other sudden signs of stroke (Red Cross, American Stroke Association): numbness or weakness of the face, arm or leg, especially on one side; confusion or trouble understanding others; trouble seeing in one or both eyes; dizziness, loss of balance or trouble walking; a sudden severe headache with no known cause; drooling or trouble swallowing; loss of responsiveness.

Signs that go away within minutes still count. They may be a transient ischaemic attack (TIA, a warning stroke); more than 10 percent of people with a TIA have a stroke within 3 months, so they need medical care now even if they feel normal again (Red Cross; American Stroke Association: call 911 even if the symptoms go away).

Children: adult stroke checks such as FAST are not proven in children (AHA 2024); suspect stroke in a child with sudden new nervous-system signs, and get help the same way. In children a stroke can show up as seizures, especially under 1 year of age (AHA 2024).

steps.text: Note the time the signs started, or the last time they were seen well. Write it down.
steps.detail:
Red Cross: note when the signs started, or when the person was last known to be well. Hospital treatments depend on this time: clot-dissolving medicine must be started within 4 1/2 hours of the first symptoms, and sooner is better (MedlinePlus).

If they woke up with the signs, the time is when they were last seen well before sleep. Give the time to whoever takes over their care.

steps.text: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Start evacuating now: stroke treatment works only within hours.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (Class 1): if stroke is suspected, activate the emergency response system immediately. Prompt medical care may reduce disability (Red Cross).

Off-grid, every hour counts. Plan the fastest way to a hospital and start now. A person with stroke signs may be weak on one side, dizzy or unsteady: do not let them walk alone, and expect to carry them or use a vehicle.

steps.text: No aspirin. Give no other food, drink or medicine for now (see detail). Sugar for possible low blood sugar is covered in the next steps.
steps.warn: No aspirin: some strokes are bleeding in the brain, and aspirin can make a bleeding stroke worse.
steps.detail:
Aspirin: the American Stroke Association advises against taking aspirin during a stroke, because some strokes are caused by a burst blood vessel rather than a clot, and aspirin could make those bleeding strokes more severe. The aspirin advice in the Chest pain or heart attack protocol does not apply here.

Other food, drink and medicine: none of the sources opened (AHA 2024, Red Cross Stroke, MedlinePlus Stroke, American Stroke Association) states a nothing-by-mouth rule for stroke. Drooling and trouble swallowing are stroke signs (Red Cross), so anything by mouth could be choked on; holding back other food, drink and medicine is a group judgement based on that risk.

Sugar is the exception, because low blood sugar is a common stroke look-alike (AHA 2024): the next steps give it to someone with diabetes, or with a measured low reading, who is fully awake and can swallow safely.

steps.text: Do you have a blood glucose meter (for example, theirs if they have diabetes)?
steps.detail: Low blood sugar is a common look-alike of stroke (AHA 2024). AHA 2024 (Class 2a): if a meter is available and using it does not delay getting help, it is reasonable to check the blood sugar of an adult with suspected stroke.

ask.q: Is a blood glucose meter available?

steps.text: Check their blood sugar, without delaying help. Is it below 70 mg/dL?
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (6.2, Class 2a): it is reasonable to check blood sugar in an adult with suspected stroke if a meter is available and it does not delay activating EMS. AHA 2024 (6.7) defines low blood sugar as below 70 mg/dL.

A normal reading does not change anything: keep treating this as a stroke and keep evacuating.

steps.text: Do they have diabetes treated with insulin or diabetes pills?
steps.detail: Low blood sugar is a common stroke look-alike (AHA 2024), and in someone with diabetes it can come from a missed meal, more exercise than usual, vomiting, or too much diabetes medicine (Red Cross). Red Cross: if you cannot tell whether their sugar is low or high, it is good to give some sugar; it can be lifesaving if low and will not do major harm if high. Check their pockets and kit, and look for a medical ID.

ask.q: Do they have diabetes treated with insulin or pills?

steps.text: Are they fully awake, answering you and following simple requests?
steps.detail: AHA 2024 (6.7, Class 3: Harm): no sugar by mouth for someone who is not awake or cannot swallow; they could choke or inhale it. "Fully awake" is the app's stricter wording, as in the Low blood sugar protocol.

steps.text: Can they swallow safely: no choking, coughing on swallowing or drooling?
steps.detail: Drooling and trouble swallowing are stroke signs (Red Cross). If in doubt, answer No: nothing by mouth.

steps.text: Give at least 20 grams of sugar: glucose tablets or gel, 7 oz orange juice, 20 to 25 Skittles or 10 to 20 jellybeans. Keep evacuating as a stroke.
steps.warn: Stop giving anything by mouth if they become drowsy, choke or start drooling: lie them on their side.
steps.detail:
This is the same rule as the sugar step of the Low blood sugar protocol. AHA 2024 (6.7, Class 1): encourage oral glucose for a person with suspected low blood sugar who is awake and able to swallow; Class 3 (Harm): not for someone who is not awake or cannot swallow. The previous two questions use the app's stricter "fully awake", as the Low blood sugar protocol does. The amounts that give about 20 grams are from the Red Cross Diabetic Emergencies page; glucose tablets or gel are preferred (AHA 2024); check the packet for 20 grams. No diet drinks.

Keep evacuating as for a stroke whatever happens: even if the signs improve after sugar, a stroke has not been ruled out. Tell the people taking over that sugar was given and when.

steps.text: Nothing by mouth if they are not fully awake or cannot swallow safely. If not fully awake, drooling or having trouble swallowing, lie them on their side (Recovery position protocol). Reassure them.
steps.detail:
Red Cross: place them in the recovery position if they are responsive but not fully awake, are drooling or have trouble swallowing. Keep them from getting cold or overheated, and give care for shock if needed (Shock protocol).

A person having a stroke may not be able to speak but may still understand you. Speak slowly and calmly, tell them what you are doing, and tell them help is coming (Red Cross).

Otherwise let them rest in a comfortable position. Watch for changes in breathing and responsiveness.

steps.text: Stay with them and keep watching breathing and responsiveness.

ask.q: Have they become unresponsive and stopped breathing normally?

steps.text: Keep evacuating, even if the signs get better. Keep watching their breathing and alertness on the way.
steps.detail:
Signs that fade or go away still need medical care now (Red Cross, American Stroke Association).

If they become drowsy or start vomiting, lie them on their side (Recovery position protocol). If they stop breathing normally, start CPR (CPR, adult protocol). If they have a seizure, use the Seizure protocol.

Tell the people who take over the time the signs started (or when they were last seen well), any blood sugar reading, and any sugar given and when.

steps.text: Start CPR now: use the CPR, adult protocol (or CPR, child or CPR, infant).
steps.detail: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

donts: Do not give aspirin; some strokes are bleeding strokes (American Stroke Association).

Do not give food, drink or medicine by mouth other than sugar for possible low blood sugar (group judgement: drooling and trouble swallowing are stroke signs); never anything by mouth if they are not fully awake or cannot swallow safely (AHA 2024).
Do not wait to see whether the signs go away; signs that go away still need care now.
Do not let them walk alone.
evacuate: Start evacuating now for any sudden stroke sign, even if it goes away (AHA 2024: activate EMS immediately). Hospital clot-dissolving treatment must start within 4 1/2 hours of the first symptoms (MedlinePlus).
Tell the receiving team when the signs started, or when the person was last seen well.
notes: FAST: Face drooping, Arm drifting down, Speech slurred or wrong, Time to get help and note when the signs began. No aspirin. Sugar only if they have diabetes or a low reading and are fully awake and swallow safely.
